title: Learning to Be Silent
text:
Four students of the Tendai school of Buddhism, who were close friends, made a vow together. For seven days they would keep complete silence as part of their meditation.

On the first day all four sat quietly. That night, as it grew dark and the oil lamps began to grow dim, one of the students could not help himself. He told a servant to fix the lamps.

The second student was surprised to hear the first one speak. He reminded him that they were not supposed to say a word.

The third student turned to the other two. Why are you two talking? he asked them.

The fourth student then remarked, with some satisfaction, that he was the only one who had not spoken.

And so, within the first day, all four had broken their vow, each one in the act of noticing someone else.
lesson: Be careful when you rush to correct a teammate, since you may be breaking the same rule while you do it. Keeping your own commitment does more good than policing others.
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919), Learning to Be Silent
